what: Matador Resources drills for oil and natural gas in the Delaware Basin of New Mexico and West Texas, the most productive part of the Permian. It also owns a midstream business, San Mateo, that gathers, processes and disposes of water and gas from its own wells and from other producers.
customers: Refiners, processors and commodity traders for the oil and gas; other producers in the basin for the midstream services.
money: Crude and associated gas from Delaware Basin wells.
Gathering, processing and water handling through San Mateo, including fees from third-party producers.
moat: Two things set Matador apart from a plain shale producer. Its acreage sits in the core of the Delaware Basin, which is the best rock in the best basin, and it owns the pipes and water infrastructure its own wells depend on, so it is not waiting in another company’s queue for capacity. That midstream ownership also earns fees from neighbours, which is a steadier income than selling barrels.
risks: Oil prices decide the result, and revenue has swung from $3.2B in 2022 to $2.8B in 2023 and back to $3.7B.
Debt is about $3.5B against only $15.3M of cash, which is a thin cushion for a commodity producer.
Water disposal in the Permian is an increasing constraint, with seismic activity leading regulators to restrict injection in parts of the basin.
Shale wells decline quickly, so a large part of the cash flow must be reinvested every year to hold production steady.
New Mexico’s regulatory and tax regime differs from Texas’s and has been less predictable.
opportunities: Free cash flow of about $2.5B against a $6.1B market value is a very large yield, and the shares trade at about 2.5 times free cash flow and 4.5 times EV/EBITDA.
The midstream business earns fee income from third parties, which is worth a higher multiple than production and could be separated or sold.
Twenty analysts average a $70.30 target, about 42% above the current price.
Core Delaware acreage has the lowest cost per barrel in American onshore oil, which means it keeps generating cash at prices where other basins stop.
watch: Free cash flow after debt reduction, and water handling capacity. The rock is excellent and the cost position is proven; the balance sheet and the ability to dispose of produced water are what could constrain it.
view: Among mid-sized American oil producers, Matador has two things most of its peers do not, and both are worth more than they look. The first is location: core Delaware Basin acreage, which is simply the best rock in American onshore oil, with the lowest cost per barrel. In a commodity business where nobody can control the price they receive, the only durable advantage is the cost of production, and Matador’s is at the right end of the curve. It keeps generating cash at oil prices that force higher-cost producers to stop drilling.

The second is San Mateo, the midstream arm. Most shale producers depend on someone else’s pipelines and water disposal, which means waiting in a queue and paying a fee. Matador owns its own, which removes a constraint on its drilling pace and turns a cost into a revenue line, because neighbouring producers pay to use it. Fee-based midstream income is worth a substantially higher multiple than production income, and it is buried inside a company the market prices as a plain oil producer. That is the part of this story I would spend the most time on, and the most likely source of a re-rating if it were ever separated.

At 2.5 times free cash flow and 4.5 times EV/EBITDA, the price assumes oil falls and stays down. Maybe it does — that is the nature of the business and nobody should pretend to know. But $2.5 billion of trailing free cash flow against a $6.1 billion market value gives a great deal of room to be wrong about the oil price, provided the balance sheet holds. And there is the one thing I would watch closely: $3.5 billion of debt against $15 million of cash is thin. It is serviceable at current prices and uncomfortable at much lower ones.

The underappreciated operational risk is water. Permian wells produce several barrels of water for every barrel of oil, disposal happens by injection, and injection has been linked to seismic activity, which has already led regulators to restrict it in parts of the basin. Owning the water infrastructure helps Matador more than most, but it does not exempt it. Watch free cash flow going to debt reduction and watch water handling capacity; the twenty analysts at $70.30 are modelling the oil price, which is the one thing none of them know.
bull: Oil holds, the lowest-cost rock in the Permian keeps throwing off cash, debt comes down fast, and the midstream arm is eventually valued separately at a midstream multiple.
bear: Oil falls for an extended period against $3.5 billion of debt and almost no cash, while water disposal limits in the Permian constrain how fast the wells can be drilled.
